intro: In 1763, most colonists were proud to be British. They celebrated the king's birthday and cheered Britain's victory over France. Just 13 years later, many of those same people declared that they no longer belonged to the British Empire. Within 30 years, they had fought a long war, won their independence and written a new plan of government that is still in use today.

This unit tells how that happened. It begins with arguments over taxes and rights, moves through eight years of war, and ends in a hot meeting room in Philadelphia where delegates designed a new kind of government. Along the way you will meet farmers, printers, soldiers, spies and lawmakers, including women, African Americans and Native nations whose choices shaped the outcome.

The founders spoke of liberty and equality, but in 1791 those ideals did not reach everyone. Enslaved people, women and Native Americans were largely left out. As you read, look for both sides of the story: the bold new ideas about rights and self-government, and the people who were still waiting for those ideas to include them.
bigQuestion: How did the American colonies become one nation, and how well did the new nation live up to its promise of liberty?

title: A New Nation

chapters.title: The Road to Revolution
chapters.bigQuestion: How did loyal British colonists become people ready to fight for independence?

story.title: Two Lanterns and a Fast Horse
story.kicker: On a cold spring night in 1775, a warning raced from Boston into the Massachusetts countryside.
paragraphs: Boston, April 18, 1775. The streets were dark and quiet, but the town was nervous. British soldiers, called Regulars, had been living in Boston for years. Now they were getting ready to march. Patriot leaders guessed where they were headed: the town of Concord, about 18 miles away. Colonists had hidden guns and gunpowder there.

Dr. Joseph Warren, a Patriot leader in Boston, sent two riders to spread the alarm. One was Paul Revere, a silversmith. The other was William Dawes, a shoemaker. Dawes slipped out of town by land. Revere had planned a signal ahead of time. Two lanterns hung in the steeple of the Old North Church meant the soldiers were crossing the Charles River by boat. Friends across the river saw the lights.

Revere was rowed quietly across the river past a British warship. On the other side, he borrowed a horse and galloped toward Lexington. He stopped at houses along the way to warn the militia, the local citizen soldiers. He probably did not shout “The British are coming!” Most colonists still thought of themselves as British. He more likely warned that “the Regulars” were coming out.

In Lexington, Revere warned two Patriot leaders, Samuel Adams and John Hancock. Dawes arrived soon after. The two men rode on toward Concord with a third rider, Dr. Samuel Prescott. A British patrol stopped them on the road. Revere was captured for a time. Dawes escaped. Prescott jumped his horse over a wall and carried the warning to Concord.

Revere and Dawes were not alone. Other riders fanned out. Church bells rang. Drums beat. By dawn on April 19, militiamen from many towns were grabbing their muskets. On the green in Lexington, a small group of them faced the British soldiers. Someone fired. No one knows who. The first battle of the American Revolution had begun.
story.think: Paul Revere is famous, but many riders spread the alarm that night. Why do you think some people become famous in history while others are forgotten?

lessons.title: A Line on the Map
lessons.mainIdea: After winning the French and Indian War, Britain tried to stop colonists from settling west of the Appalachian Mountains.
reading: In 1763, Britain won the French and Indian War. France gave up its lands in North America. British colonists were proud. Many hoped to move west into the rich lands of the Ohio River valley. But those lands were not empty. Native nations such as the Shawnee, Delaware and Odawa lived there.

Native nations did not want settlers pouring onto their lands. In 1763, an Odawa leader named Pontiac led many nations in a war against British forts around the Great Lakes. The fighting was costly for everyone. British leaders wanted to avoid another expensive war.

So King George III issued the *Proclamation of 1763*. It drew a line along the Appalachian Mountains. Colonists were not allowed to settle west of that line. Settlers who were already there were told to leave. Many colonists were angry. They felt they had fought the war to win those lands. Now their own government was blocking them. The line was hard to enforce, and many settlers crossed it anyway.

the edge of settled land, where colonists' towns met Native lands

lessons.title: Parliament Wants Money
lessons.mainIdea: To pay its war debts, Britain's Parliament began taxing the colonies directly, starting with the Sugar Act and the Stamp Act.
reading: The French and Indian War left Britain with a huge debt. Britain also planned to keep about 10,000 soldiers in North America to guard the frontier. Someone had to pay for all this. Leaders in *Parliament*, Britain's lawmaking body, decided the colonists should pay a share. After all, the war had protected them.

In 1764, Parliament passed the Sugar Act. It actually lowered the tax on molasses, a sweet syrup used to make rum. But this time Britain meant to collect the tax. For years, colonial merchants had avoided such taxes by smuggling. Now smugglers could be tried in special courts without a jury.

In 1765, Parliament passed the *Stamp Act*. It taxed printed paper. Newspapers, pamphlets, legal documents and even playing cards needed an official stamp to show the tax was paid. This tax touched almost everyone, from lawyers to printers to ordinary shoppers. It was also the first direct tax Parliament placed on the colonies. Many colonists thought it crossed a line.

a 1765 British law that taxed printed paper in the colonies

Molasses shipped from the West Indies

check.why: The Stamp Act required a paid stamp on printed papers of many kinds.

choices: It was a direct tax that touched almost everyone.
It banned newspapers completely.
It was passed by the colonial assemblies.
It only affected a few rich merchants.
check.why: Because it taxed everyday printed items, it affected people in nearly every job and town.

lessons.title: No Taxation Without Representation
lessons.mainIdea: Colonists argued that only their own elected assemblies could tax them, and their protests forced Parliament to repeal the Stamp Act.
reading: Colonists did not object to every law from Britain. They objected to being taxed by a body they did not elect. Colonists had no members in Parliament. They believed that, as British subjects, they had the right to be taxed only by their own *representatives*, such as the elected assemblies in each colony. Their slogan became “No taxation without representation.”

In October 1765, delegates from nine colonies met in New York at the Stamp Act Congress. They sent a respectful message to the king and Parliament. It said the colonists were loyal subjects, but that only their own assemblies could tax them. It was one of the first times several colonies acted together.

Protest also filled the streets. Groups called the Sons of Liberty scared stamp collectors into quitting. Merchants joined a *boycott*, refusing to buy British goods. British merchants lost money and begged Parliament for help. In 1766, Parliament repealed, or canceled, the Stamp Act. But on the same day it passed the Declaratory Act. That law said Parliament had full power to make laws for the colonies. The argument was not over.

refusing to buy or use something as a form of protest

look.title: The Stamp Act Congress Speaks
look.text: We are loyal subjects of the king and have all the rights of people born in Britain. One of those rights is that no tax may be placed on people without their own consent. We are not represented in Parliament, and because of the distance we cannot be. So only our own colonial assemblies can lawfully tax us.

check.why: Boycotts cut sales of British goods, so British merchants pressured Parliament to cancel the tax.

check.why: Even while repealing the tax, Parliament declared it could make any laws for the colonies.

lessons.title: New Taxes, New Boycotts
lessons.mainIdea: When Parliament taxed everyday imports in 1767, colonists, including many women, answered with boycotts and homemade goods.
reading: In 1767, Parliament tried again. The *Townshend Acts* taxed goods the colonies imported from Britain, including glass, lead, paint, paper and tea. Some of the money would pay the salaries of royal governors and judges. That worried colonists. If Britain paid these officials, colonial assemblies would lose power over them.

Colonists returned to boycotts. Merchants in many towns signed agreements not to import British goods. Women played a big part, because they bought much of what families used. Groups called the Daughters of Liberty held spinning bees, where women spun thread together to make homespun cloth. Wearing homemade cloth instead of British fabric became a sign of patriotism.

In 1768, Britain sent soldiers to Boston to keep order and protect tax collectors. Many Bostonians resented having armed troops in their streets. Soldiers and townspeople often insulted each other. Some off-duty soldiers took part-time jobs, which made local workers angry. Tension grew. In 1770, Parliament canceled most of the Townshend taxes. It kept one, the tax on tea, to show it still had the right to tax.

words.d: 1767 British laws that taxed glass, lead, paint, paper and tea brought into the colonies
cloth spun and woven at home instead of bought from Britain
love for and loyalty to one's country or cause

look.text: In the 1760s, women could not vote or hold office in the colonies. Yet many joined the protests by refusing to buy British cloth and tea, and by spinning and weaving at home. Choosing what to buy, and what not to buy, became a way to speak up.

Imported goods such as glass, paint, paper and tea
Furs traded with Native nations

They wrote new tax laws for Parliament.
They sold British tea in their shops.
They served as soldiers in the British army.
check.why: Spinning and weaving at home replaced British cloth and made the boycott work.

choices: Because tea was the only thing colonists bought
Because colonists asked to keep it
To pay for the Boston Massacre trial
To show it still had the right to tax the colonies
check.why: Parliament dropped the other taxes but kept one to prove its power to tax.

lessons.title: Blood on King Street
lessons.mainIdea: In 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston, killing five people, and Patriots used the event to turn opinion against Britain.
reading: On the cold night of March 5, 1770, a crowd gathered around a British guard on King Street in Boston. People shouted insults and threw snowballs and chunks of ice. More soldiers arrived. In the confusion, the soldiers fired into the crowd. Five colonists died. One of them was Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Native American ancestry. He is often remembered as one of the first people to die in the struggle for American independence.

Patriots called the shooting the *Boston Massacre*. A massacre is the killing of people who cannot defend themselves. Paul Revere made an engraving of the event. It showed soldiers calmly firing on peaceful townspeople. That was not exactly what happened, but the picture spread quickly. It was *propaganda*, information shaped to persuade people to take a side.

The soldiers were put on trial. Their lawyer was John Adams, a Patriot. He believed every person deserved a fair trial, even an unpopular one. Adams argued that the soldiers had feared for their lives. Most of them were found not guilty. Two were convicted of a lesser crime. The trial showed that colonists valued the rule of law, even when they were angry.

information shaped to persuade people to believe one side
the idea that everyone, including the government, must follow the law

Witnesses at the trial described a noisy, crowded, confusing scene, with people shouting and throwing things. Revere's picture was printed and sold across the colonies.
look.prompt: Why might Revere have shown the event the way he did? How can a picture be powerful even when it is not fully accurate?

It shaped the event to turn people against the British.

check.why: The engraving showed calm soldiers firing on peaceful people to stir anger at Britain.

lessons.title: Tea in the Harbor
lessons.mainIdea: Committees linked the colonies, and when Britain passed the Tea Act, Boston Patriots dumped a shipload of taxed tea into the harbor.
reading: Patriots knew they were stronger together. In 1772, Samuel Adams helped start a *Committee of Correspondence* in Boston. These committees wrote letters to share news and plan protests. Soon committees spread through many towns and colonies. Before phones or the internet, this letter network helped the colonies think and act as one.

In 1773, Parliament passed the Tea Act. It was meant to help the British East India Company, which had too much tea and was losing money. The law let the company sell tea directly to the colonies. The tea was actually cheaper, but it still carried the tax. Patriots saw a trick. If colonists bought the cheap tea, they would be accepting Parliament's right to tax them.

Colonists in several ports refused to let the tea be unloaded. In Boston, the governor insisted the tea come ashore. On the night of December 16, 1773, a group of men, some dressed as Mohawk people, boarded three ships. They broke open 342 chests of tea and dumped them into Boston Harbor. This protest became known as the *Boston Tea Party*. Some colonists cheered. Others thought destroying property went too far.

words.d: a group that wrote letters to share news and plan protests among towns and colonies
the 1773 protest in which colonists dumped British tea into Boston Harbor

check.why: On December 16, 1773, colonists boarded ships and threw 342 chests of tea into the harbor.

lessons.title: Britain Cracks Down
lessons.mainIdea: Parliament punished Massachusetts with harsh laws in 1774, and the colonies responded by meeting together in the First Continental Congress.
reading: Britain's leaders were furious about the tea. In 1774, Parliament passed laws to punish Boston and Massachusetts. Colonists called them the *Intolerable Acts*, meaning laws that could not be put up with. One law closed Boston's port until the tea was paid for. Another cut the power of the Massachusetts assembly and limited town meetings. Another let royal officials be tried in Britain instead of in the colony. A new Quartering Act allowed troops to be housed in colonial buildings.

General Thomas Gage, commander of British forces in North America, became governor of Massachusetts. With the port closed, Boston's trade stopped and many people lost work. Other colonies sent food and supplies to help. Britain had hoped to isolate Boston. Instead, the punishment pulled the colonies closer together.

In September 1774, delegates from 12 colonies met in Philadelphia. Only Georgia did not send anyone. This meeting was the *First Continental Congress*. Delegates included George Washington, John Adams and Samuel Adams. They agreed to stop trade with Britain. They urged colonies to train their militias. They also agreed to meet again in May 1775 if Britain did not change course.

words.d: the colonists' name for harsh 1774 laws that punished Massachusetts
the 1774 meeting in Philadelphia where delegates from 12 colonies planned a united response to Britain
a person chosen to represent a group at a meeting

It lowered the tax on tea.

check.why: The port stayed closed to trade as punishment for the Boston Tea Party.

They sent supplies to Boston and met together in Congress.
They agreed Boston deserved to be punished.

check.why: The punishment united the colonies, who helped Boston and formed the First Continental Congress.

choices: Massachusetts
Georgia
Virginia
Pennsylvania
check.why: Twelve colonies met in Philadelphia in 1774; Georgia did not send delegates.

lessons.title: The Shot Heard Round the World
lessons.mainIdea: On April 19, 1775, fighting at Lexington and Concord turned the long argument with Britain into a war.
reading: By 1775, many Massachusetts towns had trained *minutemen*. These were militia members ready to fight at a minute's notice. They stored guns and gunpowder in towns such as Concord. General Gage decided to seize those supplies. On the night of April 18, about 700 British soldiers set out from Boston.

Riders spread the alarm. At dawn on April 19, the soldiers reached Lexington. About 70 militiamen stood on the town green. Someone fired a shot. No one knows who fired first. The British soldiers then fired, and eight militiamen were killed. The British marched on to Concord.

At Concord, the soldiers found only a few supplies. At the North Bridge, they clashed with hundreds of militiamen, who forced them back. On the long march back to Boston, the British were attacked from behind trees, walls and houses. By the end of the day, the British had lost many more men than the colonists. Thousands of militiamen then surrounded Boston. The *American Revolution*, the war for independence, had begun.

words.d: colonial militia members trained to be ready to fight at a minute's notice
an army of ordinary citizens who train to fight when needed
the war and movement in which the colonies won independence from Britain

choices: To seize the colonists' guns and gunpowder
To collect the tea tax
To arrest George Washington
To sign a peace treaty
check.why: General Gage wanted to capture the military supplies stored in Concord.

check.q: What do historians know about the first shot at Lexington?

A British general fired it.
It was fired from a ship.
No one knows who fired it.
check.why: Accounts disagree, and historians still do not know who fired first.

Parliament closed the Continental Congress.
Thousands of militiamen surrounded Boston and war began.

check.why: After Lexington and Concord, militias gathered around Boston and the Revolution began.

lessons.title: One Last Try for Peace
lessons.mainIdea: The Second Continental Congress prepared for war while still offering the king a chance at peace, which he rejected.
reading: In May 1775, the *Second Continental Congress* met in Philadelphia. The fighting had already started. Congress now had to act like a government. It created the Continental Army and chose George Washington of Virginia to lead it. Washington had fought in the French and Indian War and was widely respected.

Around the same time, colonial forces led by Ethan Allen and Benedict Arnold captured Fort Ticonderoga in New York. Its cannons would later help the Americans. Still, many delegates did not want to break away from Britain. They hoped the king would take their side against Parliament.

In July 1775, Congress sent the king the *Olive Branch Petition*. An olive branch is a symbol of peace. The petition said the colonists were loyal and asked the king to help end the fighting. King George III refused to read it. Instead, he declared that the colonies were in rebellion. For many colonists, the king's answer showed that peace on fair terms was not possible.

lessons.title: A Pamphlet Changes Minds
lessons.mainIdea: Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense convinced many colonists in 1776 that independence was the right choice.
reading: Even after a year of fighting, many colonists hoped to stay part of the British Empire. Then, in January 1776, a writer named Thomas Paine published a *pamphlet*, a short booklet, called Common Sense. Paine had come to Philadelphia from England only about a year before.

Paine wrote in plain, bold language that ordinary people could understand. He attacked the idea of kings. He said it made no sense for a small island to rule a whole continent across an ocean. He argued that the colonies would be better off as an independent *republic*, a nation where people choose their leaders.

Common Sense sold widely and was read aloud in homes, taverns and army camps. People who could not read heard its arguments. It did not change every mind, but it helped turn many colonists toward independence. Within months, colony after colony told its delegates in Congress to support a break with Britain.

lessons.title: Jefferson Writes the Declaration
lessons.mainIdea: In July 1776, Congress approved the Declaration of Independence, which explained why the colonies were breaking from Britain.
reading: In June 1776, Richard Henry Lee of Virginia asked Congress to declare the colonies independent. Congress chose a committee of five to write a statement explaining the decision. The group included Thomas Jefferson, John Adams and Benjamin Franklin. Jefferson, a 33-year-old Virginian, wrote the first draft. The others suggested changes.

On July 2, 1776, Congress voted for independence. On July 4, it approved the final wording of the *Declaration of Independence*. The document has four main parts. It opens by explaining why a statement is needed. Next it describes people's natural rights. Then it lists many complaints, or *grievances*, against the king. Finally, it declares the colonies free and independent states.

The most famous part is about rights. It says all people have *unalienable rights*, rights that cannot be taken away, including life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. It says governments get their power from the consent of the governed. If a government destroys people's rights, the people may change it or replace it. These ideas came partly from Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke.

words.d: the 1776 document in which the colonies announced their break from Britain and explained why

lessons.title: Who Was Left Out?
lessons.mainIdea: The Declaration said all men are created equal, but in 1776 those words did not apply to enslaved people, women or Native Americans.
reading: The Declaration's words were bold, but they did not match life in 1776. About one in five people in the colonies was enslaved. Jefferson himself enslaved hundreds of people over his lifetime. His first draft blamed the king for the slave trade, but Congress removed that section. Some delegates' home colonies depended on slavery.

Women were not mentioned. They could not vote, and married women usually could not own property in their own names. Native Americans appear in the Declaration only in a complaint that the king had turned them against the colonists. Native nations were fighting to protect their own lands and freedom.

Still, the Declaration's promise lasted. Over time, many groups used its words to demand their rights. Enslaved people in Massachusetts cited the ideas of liberty when they asked for freedom. Later, abolitionists, women's rights leaders and civil rights leaders quoted it. The gap between the Declaration's *ideals* and reality became a challenge that Americans have worked on ever since.

chapters.title: The American Revolution
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a new nation with a small, poorly supplied army defeat the most powerful empire in the world?

story.title: A Winter of Huts and Hunger
story.kicker: In the winter of 1777, the Continental Army nearly fell apart at Valley Forge, and came out of it stronger.
paragraphs: December 19, 1777. About 12,000 tired soldiers marched into a place called Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, about 20 miles from Philadelphia. The British had captured Philadelphia that fall. Congress had fled the city. George Washington chose Valley Forge because it was close enough to watch the British, and high ground made it easier to defend.

There were no buildings for the army. The soldiers had to build their own shelter. They cut down trees and built rows of log huts. Each hut held about 12 men, packed around a small fireplace. Smoke filled the air. Many soldiers had no shoes and wrapped their feet in rags. Blankets were scarce. Some days there was little to eat except “firecake,” a flat bread of flour and water cooked on hot stones.

The biggest danger was not the cold. It was disease. Illnesses such as typhus and dysentery spread quickly through the crowded camp. Nearly 2,000 soldiers died during the months at Valley Forge, most of them from sickness. Washington begged Congress and the states for food and clothing. Supplies came slowly, partly because the new government had little money and poor ways to move goods.

In February 1778, a Prussian officer named Friedrich von Steuben arrived. He spoke little English, but he knew how to train soldiers. He drilled a small group of men until they could march, load and fight together. Then those men trained others. Day after day, the army practiced on the frozen fields. Slowly, a group of separate units became one army.

In May 1778, wonderful news reached the camp: France had agreed to fight alongside the Americans. The soldiers held a celebration with cheering and cannon salutes. In June, the army marched out of Valley Forge to chase the British, who were leaving Philadelphia. The men who marched out were thinner, but they were tougher, better trained and more confident than the men who had marched in.
story.think: Many soldiers could have gone home that winter, but most stayed. What do you think kept them at Valley Forge?

lessons.title: Bunker Hill and Boston
lessons.mainIdea: The Battle of Bunker Hill showed that colonial soldiers could stand up to the British army, and in 1776 the British left Boston.
reading: After Lexington and Concord, thousands of militiamen surrounded British troops in Boston. In June 1775, colonists built earthworks, walls of dirt, on Breed's Hill, near Bunker Hill, overlooking the city. On June 17, British soldiers marched up the hill in tight lines to drive them off.

Twice the colonists pushed the British back. On the third attack, the colonists ran low on gunpowder and had to retreat. The British won the hill, but more than 1,000 of their soldiers were killed or wounded. The colonists lost far fewer. The fight became known as the *Battle of Bunker Hill*. Black soldiers, including Peter Salem and Salem Poor, fought bravely there.

In July 1775, George Washington arrived to take command of the new *Continental Army*. He needed heavy guns. That winter, a bookseller turned officer named Henry Knox led a team that dragged dozens of heavy cannons hundreds of miles over snow from Fort Ticonderoga. In March 1776, the cannons appeared on hills above Boston. The British saw they could not hold the city. They sailed away.

lessons.title: Patriots, Loyalists and Native Nations
lessons.mainIdea: Americans were deeply divided about the war, and Native nations made hard choices to protect their own lands.
reading: Not every colonist wanted independence. *Patriots* supported the war against Britain. *Loyalists*, sometimes called Tories, stayed loyal to the king. Historians estimate that perhaps one in five white colonists was a Loyalist. Many others tried to stay *neutral*, not taking either side. Families and neighbors were sometimes split.

People became Loyalists for many reasons. Some worked for the British government or depended on trade with Britain. Some feared chaos without a king. Others belonged to groups that hoped Britain would protect them. Patriots often treated Loyalists harshly, taking their property or driving them out. By the war's end, tens of thousands of Loyalists had left, many for Canada or Britain.

Most Native nations saw the Americans, who wanted their lands, as the bigger threat. Many sided with Britain. The Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois Confederacy, split apart. The Mohawk leader Joseph Brant led warriors on the British side. The Oneida and Tuscarora mostly helped the Americans. In 1779, American troops burned dozens of Haudenosaunee towns and crops in New York. The war was a disaster for many Native communities, no matter which side they chose.

colonists who stayed loyal to the British king during the Revolution
not taking either side in a conflict

The British king once tried to stop settlers at the Appalachian Mountains. Now both sides want your warriors' help, or at least your promise to stay out of the fight.

lessons.title: Retreat, Then Surprise
lessons.mainIdea: After losing New York in 1776, Washington's army won surprise victories at Trenton and Princeton that kept the Revolution alive.
reading: In the summer of 1776, Britain sent a huge force of ships and soldiers to New York. In August, the British beat Washington's army on Long Island. Washington's troops escaped across the East River at night. But the British captured New York City, and they held it for the rest of the war. The Americans retreated across New Jersey into Pennsylvania.

By December, the army was shrinking. Many soldiers' terms of service would end on December 31. Some had already gone home. Thomas Paine, now traveling with the army, wrote a new essay called The American Crisis to lift people's spirits. Washington knew he needed a victory, fast.

On Christmas night, 1776, Washington led about 2,400 men across the icy Delaware River in boats. In the early morning, they attacked *Hessians* at Trenton, New Jersey. Hessians were German soldiers hired by Britain. The surprise attack worked, and the Americans captured most of the Hessian force. A few days later, on January 3, 1777, Washington won again at Princeton. These small wins gave Americans new hope and convinced many soldiers to *reenlist*.

lessons.title: Victory at Saratoga
lessons.mainIdea: The American victory at Saratoga in 1777 was a turning point because it convinced France to join the war.
reading: In 1777, the British made a plan to cut the colonies in two. General John Burgoyne would march south from Canada into New York. Other British forces were supposed to meet him. If the plan worked, New England would be cut off from the other colonies.

The plan fell apart. Burgoyne's army moved slowly through thick forests. Americans chopped down trees to block roads. The main British army, under General William Howe, went to capture Philadelphia instead of helping Burgoyne. Meanwhile, American militias kept gathering to fight.

Near Saratoga, New York, American forces under General Horatio Gates fought Burgoyne's army in two battles. Benedict Arnold, then an American officer, led bold attacks and was badly wounded. On October 17, 1777, Burgoyne surrendered his entire army of about 6,000 men. The *Battle of Saratoga* was a *turning point*. It proved to Europe that the Americans could win.

lessons.title: Help From Abroad
lessons.mainIdea: France, Spain and volunteers from Europe gave the Americans soldiers, ships, money and skills they badly needed.
reading: In February 1778, France signed an *alliance*, a formal agreement, with the United States. France was Britain's old rival and wanted revenge for losing the French and Indian War. France sent money, weapons, soldiers and, most important, a navy. Britain now had to fight a larger war around the world.

Spain joined the war against Britain in 1779 as an ally of France. Bernardo de Gálvez, the Spanish governor of Louisiana, led troops against British posts along the Gulf of Mexico. He captured Baton Rouge, Mobile and Pensacola. His army included soldiers from Spain, Mexico and the Caribbean, as well as free Black and Native fighters. These attacks kept British forces busy in the South.

Individual volunteers came too. The Marquis de Lafayette, a wealthy young Frenchman, arrived in 1777 at age 19. He served without pay and became like a son to Washington. Friedrich von Steuben trained the army at Valley Forge. Thaddeus Kosciuszko, an engineer from Poland, designed defenses at Saratoga and West Point. Each brought skills the young army lacked.

lessons.title: War on the Sea and in Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Americans fought at sea against the powerful British navy and on the western frontier, where George Rogers Clark captured British posts in the Illinois country.
reading: Britain had the strongest navy in the world. The Continental Navy was tiny. Congress also allowed *privateers*, privately owned ships given permission to attack enemy merchant ships. Privateers captured many British ships and their cargo.

The most famous American naval captain was John Paul Jones. In 1779, off the coast of Britain, his ship the Bonhomme Richard fought the British warship Serapis. Jones's ship was badly damaged and sinking, but he refused to give up. In the end, the British captain surrendered. Years later, Jones was reported to have said, “I have not yet begun to fight,” though no one can be sure of his exact words.

The war also reached the land that would become Illinois. British forts in the West supplied Native allies who raided American settlements. George Rogers Clark, a young officer from Virginia, led a small force down the Ohio River. On July 4, 1778, he captured the British post at Kaskaskia without firing a shot. Soon after, Cahokia joined him. In February 1779, Clark's men marched through icy, flooded land to capture Vincennes in present-day Indiana. His victories helped the United States later claim this *territory*.

lessons.title: Women in the War
lessons.mainIdea: Women kept farms and businesses running, supported the army and sometimes fought, and some began asking for rights of their own.
reading: When men went to war, women took on new work. They ran farms, shops and businesses. They raised money, sewed clothing for soldiers and kept boycotts going. Some women traveled with the army as *camp followers*. They cooked, washed clothes and nursed the sick and wounded. Martha Washington spent winters with her husband at army camps.

A few women fought. At the Battle of Monmouth in 1778, Mary Ludwig Hays carried water to soldiers and helped fire a cannon after her husband fell. Her story became part of the legend of “Molly Pitcher.” Deborah Sampson disguised herself as a man named Robert Shurtleff and joined the Continental Army in 1782. She served until an illness revealed her secret. Years later, she received a soldier's *pension*, payments given to veterans.

Abigail Adams managed the family farm in Massachusetts while her husband, John, served in Congress. Her letters show a sharp mind. In 1776, she urged him to think about women's rights in the new government. John Adams did not take her request seriously. But her words show that the Revolution's ideas about liberty made some women question their own lack of rights.

to change one's appearance to hide who one is

lessons.title: African Americans and the Fight for Freedom
lessons.mainIdea: Thousands of African Americans fought in the Revolution, some for the Americans and some for the British, most of them hoping to win their own freedom.
reading: For African Americans, the key question was which side offered freedom. In November 1775, Lord Dunmore, the royal governor of Virginia, made an offer. Enslaved people who escaped from Patriot enslavers and fought for the British would be freed. Hundreds joined him quickly. Later in the war, thousands more escaped to British lines.

At first, Washington did not want Black men in the Continental Army. Soon, the army needed more soldiers, and that changed. About 5,000 African Americans served on the American side. Some were free. Others were enslaved men promised freedom for their service. The 1st Rhode Island Regiment included many Black soldiers.

James Armistead was an enslaved man in Virginia. In 1781, with his enslaver's permission, he joined the Marquis de Lafayette as a spy. He pretended to be a runaway working for the British and sent back valuable information before the Battle of Yorktown. After the war, he was not automatically freed. In 1787, with Lafayette's support, Virginia's lawmakers granted him his *freedom*. He took the name James Armistead Lafayette.

the state of being free, not held or controlled by someone else

lessons.title: The War Moves South
lessons.mainIdea: Britain shifted the war to the South, where early British victories gave way to hard-fought American comebacks.
reading: After Saratoga, British leaders turned south. They believed many Loyalists lived there and would help them. British troops captured Savannah, Georgia, in 1778. In 1780, they took Charleston, South Carolina, and captured thousands of American soldiers. It was one of the worst American defeats of the war. Later that year, the British crushed another American army at Camden, South Carolina.

The South became a bitter fight between Patriots and Loyalists, often neighbors. Small bands of Patriots used *guerrilla warfare*, hit-and-run attacks by small groups. Francis Marion of South Carolina struck British supply lines and then disappeared into the swamps. He became known as the “Swamp Fox.”

The tide slowly turned. In October 1780, Patriot militia defeated a Loyalist force at Kings Mountain. General Nathanael Greene took command of the southern army. In January 1781, Daniel Morgan won a clever victory at Cowpens, South Carolina. Greene lost some battles, but he wore down the British army led by General Charles Cornwallis. Cornwallis moved his tired army north into Virginia, to a town called Yorktown.

words.d: fighting with small, fast groups that make surprise attacks and then escape
a large plan for how to win a war or reach a goal

look.prompt: How can an army lose battles and still win a war? Use Greene's strategy to explain.

check.why: British leaders expected strong Loyalist support in the southern colonies.

lessons.title: Yorktown and the Peace
lessons.mainIdea: With French help, Americans trapped a British army at Yorktown in 1781, and the Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognized American independence.
reading: In 1781, Washington saw a chance. Cornwallis's army was camped at Yorktown, on a peninsula in Virginia with water on three sides. A French fleet under Admiral de Grasse sailed into Chesapeake Bay and drove off British ships. Now Cornwallis could not escape by sea. Washington and the French general Rochambeau rushed their armies south from New York.

American and French troops surrounded Yorktown and bombarded the British with cannons. On October 19, 1781, Cornwallis surrendered more than 7,000 soldiers. The *Battle of Yorktown* was the last major battle of the war. In London, leaders realized that winning would cost too much. Parliament voted to stop the offensive war in America.

Peace talks took place in Paris. Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and John Jay represented the United States. The *Treaty of Paris* was signed on September 3, 1783. Britain recognized the United States as independent. The new nation's land stretched west to the Mississippi River. Native nations were not part of the talks. Britain handed over lands that Native peoples still lived on and claimed.

the 1783 peace agreement in which Britain recognized American independence
land with water on three sides

lessons.title: What the Revolution Changed
lessons.mainIdea: The Americans won through determination, leadership and foreign help, and the Revolution's ideas began to change society, though slowly and unevenly.
reading: How did the Americans win? They fought on home ground and knew the land. Britain had to send soldiers and supplies across 3,000 miles of ocean. Washington kept his army together through terrible times. France and Spain added money, troops and ships. And many Americans believed deeply in their cause and refused to give up.

The Revolution's ideas about liberty and equality began to change society. States wrote new constitutions. Some began ending slavery. Vermont's constitution of 1777 banned adult slavery. Pennsylvania passed a law in 1780 to end slavery gradually, over many years. In Massachusetts, court cases in the 1780s, brought partly by enslaved people such as Elizabeth Freeman, led to slavery's end there.

But change was uneven. In the South, slavery grew stronger after the war. Women still could not vote in most places. Native nations faced more settlers pressing west. The Revolution created a nation based on the idea of equal rights. It would take a long time, and much struggle, for that idea to reach everyone. This was the Revolution's *legacy*, what it handed down to later generations.

chapters.title: From Confederation to Constitution
chapters.bigQuestion: How did Americans create a government strong enough to work but limited enough to protect their liberty?

story.title: A Hot Summer Behind Closed Doors
story.kicker: In 1787, a group of delegates locked themselves in a room in Philadelphia and wrote a plan that still governs the nation.
paragraphs: Philadelphia, May 1787. Delegates arrived at the Pennsylvania State House, the same building where the Declaration of Independence had been approved 11 years earlier. Today we call it Independence Hall. They came from 12 states. Rhode Island refused to send anyone. Their official job was to fix the Articles of Confederation, the nation's first plan of government. Many of them planned to do much more.

Some of the most famous people in America were there. George Washington was chosen to lead the meeting. Benjamin Franklin, 81 years old, was the oldest delegate. James Madison of Virginia, a short, quiet man who had studied governments of the past, came with a plan already written. Over the summer, 55 delegates took part, though not all at the same time.

The delegates agreed to keep their talks secret. They wanted to speak freely and change their minds without newspapers reporting every word. Guards stood at the doors. Day after day, the delegates argued through a hot, sticky Philadelphia summer. Much of what we know comes from Madison, who sat near the front and took careful notes every day.

The arguments were fierce. Big states and small states fought over power. Northern and southern delegates clashed over slavery. More than once, the meeting almost fell apart. Some delegates left early. But again and again, the delegates found compromises, deals in which each side gave up something to reach an agreement.

On September 17, 1787, 39 delegates signed the finished Constitution. As the last men signed, Franklin pointed to the back of Washington's chair, which had a sun painted on it. According to Madison's notes, Franklin said he had often wondered whether the sun was rising or setting. Now, he said, he was happy to know it was a rising sun. The new plan still had to be approved by the states.
story.think: The delegates met in secret. Was that a good idea for writing a plan of government for a free people? Why or why not?

lessons.title: Writing New Rules
lessons.mainIdea: After declaring independence, each state wrote a constitution that limited government power and protected certain rights.
reading: Once the colonies declared independence, they needed new governments. Each state wrote a *constitution*, a written plan that sets out how a government works. Americans wanted their rules in writing, so leaders could not simply change them. Britain had no single written constitution, and colonists felt that had allowed Parliament to ignore their rights.

Most state constitutions kept governors weak and gave most power to elected legislatures. Americans remembered how royal governors had used their power. Many states added a *bill of rights*, a list of freedoms the government could not take away. Virginia's Declaration of Rights, written mainly by George Mason in 1776, protected freedom of the press and trial by jury.

Who could vote? In most states, only white men who owned a certain amount of property. New Jersey's 1776 constitution was unusual. It allowed property-owning women and free Black men to vote. Some did, until the state took that right away in 1807. The new states were more democratic than the colonies had been, but most people still had no voice in government.

words.d: a written plan that describes how a government is organized and what powers it has
a list of freedoms that a government promises to protect
the part of government that makes laws

look.title: Weak Governors on Purpose
look.text: Pennsylvania's first state constitution did not have a single governor at all. Instead, a council of several people shared executive power. Many Americans of the 1770s believed that one powerful leader could easily turn into a tyrant, like the king they had just rejected.
look.prompt: What are the risks of a leader with too much power? What problems might come from a leader with too little power?

choices: So leaders could not easily change the rules or ignore rights
So they could send copies to the king
Because Britain required it
Because no one could remember the laws
check.why: A written plan made government power clear and harder to abuse.

check.q: Why did most early state constitutions keep governors weak?
choices: Governors were chosen by Parliament.
No one wanted to be governor.
The Articles of Confederation banned governors.
People remembered abuses by royal governors.
check.why: Americans feared a strong executive after their experience with royal governors.

choices: Only the governor could vote.

check.why: New Jersey's constitution allowed some women and free Black men to vote until 1807.

lessons.title: The Articles of Confederation
lessons.mainIdea: The Articles of Confederation created a weak national government because Americans feared a strong central power.
reading: The Continental Congress also wrote a plan for a national government. It was called the *Articles of Confederation*. A confederation is a loose union of independent states. Congress approved the Articles in 1777, but they did not take effect until 1781. Maryland refused to approve them until states such as Virginia gave up their claims to western lands.

Under the Articles, the national government was just one body: Congress. Each state had one vote, no matter how many people lived there. There was no president to carry out laws and no national courts to settle disputes. Congress could declare war, make treaties, borrow money and run a post office.

But Congress had very little power. It could not collect taxes. It could only ask the states for money, and the states often said no. It could not control trade between states. Important laws needed the votes of 9 of the 13 states. Changing the Articles required all 13 to agree. Americans had designed a weak government on purpose. They did not want to replace one *tyranny* with another.

words.d: the first plan of government for the United States, which created a weak national Congress
a loose union of independent states
cruel and unfair use of power by a government or ruler

look.title: The States Keep Their Power
look.text: Each state retains its sovereignty, freedom, and independence, and every Power, jurisdiction and right, which is not by this confederation expressly delegated to the United States, in Congress assembled.
look.cite: Articles of Confederation, Article II, approved 1777, in effect 1781
look.prompt: According to this article, who holds most of the power: the states or the national government? What problems could that cause?

check.q: How many votes did each state have in Congress under the Articles?
choices: One for every 30,000 people
Two
One
Thirteen
check.why: Every state had a single vote regardless of its population.

choices: The power to run a post office
The power to collect taxes
The power to make treaties

check.why: Congress could only ask states for money; it could not tax people directly.

check.q: Why did Americans create such a weak national government?
choices: They feared a strong central government would become a tyranny.
They wanted the king to return.
They thought the war would never end.
They were not allowed to create a strong one.
check.why: After fighting a powerful king and Parliament, Americans distrusted strong central power.

lessons.title: Dividing the Northwest
lessons.mainIdea: Two land laws organized the Northwest Territory, including future Illinois, created a path to statehood and banned slavery there.
reading: The Articles government did have one big success: it planned for the West. The United States now owned land between the Appalachian Mountains and the Mississippi River. North of the Ohio River lay a region called the *Northwest Territory*. It would one day become Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin and part of Minnesota.

The Land Ordinance of 1785 set up a system to survey, or measure, the land. It was divided into squares called *township*s, each six miles on a side. Each township had 36 sections of one square mile. One section in every township was set aside to support public schools. You can still see this grid today in the square roads and farm fields of Illinois.

The *Northwest Ordinance* of 1787 set rules for governing the region. When an area had 60,000 free people, it could apply to become a state, equal to the original 13. Settlers were promised freedom of religion and trial by jury. The law also banned slavery in the territory, although in practice some people in Illinois were held in slavery or forced service for years afterward. The ordinance promised good faith toward Native nations, but settlers kept pushing onto their lands.

a 1787 law that set up government in the Northwest Territory, a path to statehood and a ban on slavery
a square unit of land six miles on each side, used to divide western lands

look.prompt: What does this article forbid? How might this rule have shaped the future of Illinois?

lessons.title: A Government Without Money
lessons.mainIdea: Without the power to tax or control trade, the Confederation government could not pay its debts or earn respect from other nations.
reading: The war left the nation deeply in debt. Congress owed money to soldiers, to citizens and to countries such as France. But Congress could not tax. When it asked the states for money, they sent only a small part of what was needed. Many soldiers went home without the pay they were promised.

During the war, Congress had printed paper money called Continentals. So much was printed that it lost almost all its value. People began saying something useless was “not worth a Continental.” States printed their own money, too. Some states taxed goods from other states. Trade became confusing and unfair.

Other nations saw the weakness. Britain kept soldiers in forts in the Northwest Territory, even though the peace treaty said it would leave. In 1784, Spain closed the port of New Orleans to American trade. Western farmers needed that port to ship their crops down the Mississippi River. Congress had no army or money to push back. Many leaders began to fear the new nation might fall apart.

the kind of money used in a country

look.title: Asking Instead of Taxing
look.text: Imagine a club where the leaders must pay for everything the club does, but they cannot require members to pay dues. They can only ask politely. Some members pay. Many do not. Meanwhile, the club owes money to other groups and cannot pay them back.
look.prompt: What would happen to this club over time? How is it like the government under the Articles?

choices: It became the most valuable money in the world.

check.why: Congress printed so many Continentals that they became nearly worthless.

choices: It had no power to tax and states sent little money.

check.why: Congress depended on states' contributions, which often did not come.

lessons.title: Farmers in Revolt
lessons.mainIdea: Shays's Rebellion, an armed protest by Massachusetts farmers, convinced many leaders that the national government needed to be stronger.
reading: In the 1780s, many farmers in western Massachusetts were in trouble. They owed money but had little cash. The state raised taxes to pay its war debts and demanded payment in hard money, such as gold or silver. Courts began taking farms from people who could not pay. Some farmers were even sent to jail for debt.

In 1786, angry farmers, many of them war veterans, took action. They gathered in armed groups and shut down courts so judges could not take their farms. One of their leaders was Daniel Shays, a former captain in the Continental Army. In January 1787, rebels marched on the federal *arsenal*, a storehouse for weapons, in Springfield. The state militia fired on them, and several rebels were killed. The uprising, called *Shays's Rebellion*, soon ended.

The rebellion shocked leaders across the country. Congress had no army to help Massachusetts. George Washington worried that the nation was falling into disorder. The year before, delegates from five states had met in Annapolis, Maryland, to discuss trade problems. They had called for a larger meeting in Philadelphia. After Shays's Rebellion, more states agreed to send delegates.

a place where weapons and ammunition are stored
a revolt against people in power

look.text: Many of Shays's followers had fought in the Revolution against unfair taxes from a distant government. Now they said their own state government was taking their farms with unfair taxes. State leaders called them lawbreakers who threatened order and property.
look.prompt: How were Shays's rebels like the Patriots of 1775? How were they different?

choices: They wanted to rejoin Britain.

check.why: Taxes and debt collection were costing farmers their land and freedom.

lessons.title: Two Plans for a New Government
lessons.mainIdea: At the Constitutional Convention, large states backed the Virginia Plan and small states backed the New Jersey Plan.
reading: Soon after the *Constitutional Convention* began, delegates made a bold decision. Instead of fixing the Articles, they would write a new plan. Not everyone agreed, but the idea moved forward.

The first plan came from Virginia. It was mostly the work of James Madison. The *Virginia Plan* called for three branches of government: one to make laws, one to carry them out and one to judge them. Congress would have two houses. In both, the number of representatives would depend on a state's population. That meant large states such as Virginia would have much more power.

Small states objected. They feared the big states would outvote them on everything. William Paterson of New Jersey offered another plan. The *New Jersey Plan* kept a Congress with one house, where each state had one equal vote, as under the Articles. It gave Congress some new powers, such as taxing trade. For weeks, the two sides argued, and neither would give in.

words.d: the 1787 meeting in Philadelphia where delegates wrote the U.S. Constitution
a plan giving states power in Congress based on population, favored by large states
a plan giving each state an equal vote in Congress, favored by small states

look.title: Fair to Whom?
look.text: Virginia had more than ten times as many people as Delaware. A Virginia delegate might say: “It is only fair that more people get more votes.” A Delaware delegate might answer: “We are an equal state. If votes follow population, big states will control everything.”
look.prompt: Which idea of fairness do you agree with more? Is there a way to honor both?

Representation in Congress based on population
A king for the United States
One equal vote for each state
check.why: The Virginia Plan gave more representatives to states with more people.

check.q: Why did small states prefer the New Jersey Plan?
choices: It gave each state an equal vote.
It moved the capital to New Jersey.

check.why: Equal votes protected small states from being outvoted by large ones.

check.q: Who was the main author of the Virginia Plan?

James Madison

lessons.title: The Great Compromise
lessons.mainIdea: The Great Compromise created a Congress with two houses: one based on population and one with equal votes for each state.
reading: By early July 1787, the convention was stuck. Large and small states would not budge. Some delegates feared the meeting would fail. Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth of Connecticut helped push a middle path.

Under their plan, Congress would have two houses. In the House of Representatives, each state's number of seats would depend on its population. In the Senate, every state would have two senators, no matter its size. Bills about raising money would have to start in the House. On July 16, the delegates narrowly approved this plan. It became known as the *Great Compromise*, or the Connecticut Compromise.

Each side got something it wanted, and each gave something up. That is what a *compromise* is. The Great Compromise saved the convention. Today, Congress still works this way. Illinois has 2 senators, the same as every other state, but its number of House members depends on its population.

words.d: the agreement that created a House based on population and a Senate with two members from each state
an agreement in which each side gives up something it wants
having two lawmaking houses

lessons.title: Bargains Over Slavery
lessons.mainIdea: To keep southern states in the union, delegates made compromises that protected slavery in the new Constitution.
reading: Slavery divided the delegates. Southern states had large numbers of enslaved people. They wanted them counted when deciding how many House seats a state got, even though enslaved people could not vote. Many northern delegates objected. The convention agreed that three of every five enslaved people would be counted. This was the *Three-Fifths Compromise*. It gave southern states extra power in Congress and in choosing presidents.

Delegates also argued about the *slave trade*, the business of bringing captured Africans to America to be sold. Some delegates wanted to end it. Delegates from Georgia and South Carolina threatened to leave. The compromise said Congress could not ban the trade until 1808. Congress did ban it starting in 1808, but slavery itself continued inside the country.

Another clause required that people who escaped slavery into another state be returned. The Constitution never uses the word slavery. It speaks instead of “other persons” and people “held to service.” Many delegates knew slavery clashed with the ideals of the Revolution. They chose union over ending slavery, a choice that would shape the nation's future.

lessons.title: Choosing a President
lessons.mainIdea: Delegates created the office of president and the Electoral College as a compromise over how the nation's leader would be chosen.
reading: The Articles had no leader to carry out laws. The delegates decided to create one: a *president*. The president would enforce laws, command the military and deal with other nations. But how much power should one person have? After a war against a king, the delegates did not want to create another one.

They argued about how to choose the president. Some wanted Congress to pick. Others feared that would make the president too dependent on Congress. A few wanted the people to vote directly. Others worried that voters in a huge country would not know candidates from far-off states. There was also a slavery question. The South had many people who could not vote.

The answer was the *Electoral College*. Each state chooses electors equal to its number of senators plus representatives. The electors vote for president. The president serves a four-year term. Everyone expected George Washington to be the first president. His honesty and his willingness to give up power after the war made many delegates comfortable creating the office.

lessons.title: Dividing and Checking Power
lessons.mainIdea: The Constitution divides power among three branches and between the national and state governments so that no one part becomes too strong.
reading: The Constitution begins with the Preamble, which explains its goals. Then it sets up three branches. Congress, the legislative branch, makes laws. The president leads the executive branch, which carries out laws. The Supreme Court and other courts form the judicial branch, which decides what laws mean. Splitting government this way is called *separation of powers*.

Each branch can limit the others. This is called *checks and balances*. The president can veto, or reject, a bill passed by Congress. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses. The Senate must approve the president's choices for judges and top officials. Congress can impeach, or charge, and remove a president for serious wrongdoing.

The Constitution also divides power between the national government and the states. This system is called *federalism*. Only the national government can print money, declare war or make treaties. States run elections and set up schools and local governments. Both can collect taxes. The Constitution can also be changed through amendments, but the process is hard on purpose.

lessons.title: The Fight Over Ratification
lessons.mainIdea: Federalists and Antifederalists debated the Constitution in every state before it was ratified in 1788.
reading: The Constitution would take effect only after 9 of the 13 states approved it. To *ratify* means to approve officially. Each state held a special convention to decide. A great debate broke out in newspapers, taverns and meeting halls.

Supporters were called *Federalists*. They argued that the Articles had failed and that the nation needed a stronger government to survive. Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay wrote 85 essays in New York newspapers explaining the Constitution. They signed them with the pen name Publius. Today these essays are known as The Federalist Papers.

Opponents were called *Antifederalists*. They included Patrick Henry and George Mason of Virginia. They feared a strong national government would crush the states and threaten liberty. Their biggest complaint was that the Constitution had no bill of rights. Delaware ratified first, in December 1787. In June 1788, New Hampshire became the ninth state. Votes in Massachusetts, Virginia and New York were close. Federalists won support partly by promising to add a bill of rights.

lessons.title: Adding a Bill of Rights
lessons.mainIdea: The first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, were added in 1791 to protect individual freedoms from the national government.
reading: The new government began in 1789, with George Washington as the first president. Congress met in New York City, the first capital. James Madison, now a member of the House of Representatives, kept the Federalists' promise. He drafted a list of amendments to protect people's rights.

Congress sent 12 amendments to the states. By December 1791, enough states had ratified 10 of them. These first ten *amendment*s are known as the *Bill of Rights*. The First Amendment protects freedom of religion, speech, the press and assembly, and the right to petition the government. Other amendments protect the right to a fair and speedy trial, protect against unreasonable searches, and ban cruel and unusual punishments.

The Tenth Amendment says that powers not given to the national government are kept by the states or the people. At first, the Bill of Rights limited only the national government, and it did not protect everyone equally. Enslaved people, for example, did not enjoy these rights. Over time, Americans have used the Bill of Rights to demand fair treatment for more and more people.
